The faunal assemblages from the Baxian and Naxian caves are taxonomically diverse and remarkably similar in composition (Supplementary Information 3 and Extended Data Fig. 3). Both assemblages include numerous taxa that have since become locally extinct, including Pongo, Elephas and rhinoceros Dicerorhinus, though most remain extant elsewhere in Asia. Notably, H. erectus, Stegodon and ‘Megalovis’ are globally extinct. Habitat preference analysis indicates that both assemblages are strongly dominated by forest-dwelling taxa (Supplementary Fig. 3), which is consistent with predominantly forested landscapes during the time of deposition.

Recent findings suggest that the plant-equivalent stable carbon isotope values for the Baxian faunal teeth, after correction for species-specific diet-to-enamel enrichment factors based on body mass29 (Supplementary Information 9), range from −31.5 to −23.0‰ (average = −27.6 ± 1.87‰ (1σ)), while lower values observed at the Naxian cave range from −34.0 to −25.1‰ (average = −29.4 ± 2.45‰ (1σ)). Both assemblages yield values well below the dense-canopy forest threshold of −27.5‰ (ref. 28), with no evidence of C4 plant consumption or even C3–C4 intermediate signatures (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 9). These data indicate that the fauna at both sites derived their dietary carbon exclusively from C3 vegetation, with the frequency of canopy-related values exceeding those reported for equatorial African rainforest systems29 and being comparable to that documented for western Amazonian forests30,31,32. This pattern is particularly notable given that several of the taxa represented in the assemblages are known elsewhere to exploit mixed C3–C4 resources or to incorporate substantial C4-derived inputs into their diets in more open environments16.

Recent findings suggest that independent oxygen isotope (δ18O) and clumped isotope (Δ47) analyses further support these environmental reconstructions, indicating humid tropical conditions with higher precipitation and cooler temperatures than modern values in this region (Extended Data Fig. 9 and Supplementary Information 9 and 10).

Industry observers note that three H. erectus teeth from the Naxian cave (NX-B1, NX-B2 and NX-A1) show similarly low isotopic values, with carbon values ranging from −15.0 to −14.0‰, which fall at the boundary between dense-canopy forest and more open C3 vegetation. Although the dataset is limited (n = 3) and at the moment restricted to the Naxian locality, these values are fully consistent with those observed across the much larger faunal assemblage and fall within the range expected for consumers deriving their dietary carbon from closed-canopy C3 vegetation, demonstrating that these late H. erectus populations exploited tropical rainforest resources.

In a recent development, high-resolution trace element mapping on one H. erectus individual from the Baxian cave (PA1799) yielded 87Sr/86Sr ratios ranging from 0.7110 to 0.7220 (Supplementary Information 11 and Extended Data Fig. 10), while three H. erectus teeth sampled from the Naxian cave showed overlapping but distinct ranges. All four individuals indicate either movement between geologically distinct regions or consumption of resources from multiple locations during childhood (2–6 years), corresponding to the period of tooth formation.

A regional strontium isoscape for southern China and northern Southeast Asia33 (Supplementary Information 11) reveals substantial spatial heterogeneity in predicted 87Sr/86Sr ratios, with the local Baxian–Naxian region characterized by relatively homogeneous values (0.710–0.715), reflecting the dominant Carboniferous–Permian limestone karst geology (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 10). More radiogenic signatures (0.717–0.723) occur to the west and northwest in mountainous areas underlain by Precambrian and Palaeozoic metamorphic rocks, while intermediate to more radiogenic values (0.715–0.720) characterize regions to the south, including the Red River valley of northern Vietnam.

Geographic assignment probability maps generated for three representative 87Sr/86Sr values observed in the human tooth profiles indicate that these H. erectus individuals may have moved between the local limestone karst regions and more distant areas during childhood, with the most radiogenic signatures potentially pointing towards areas as far afield as northern Vietnam, which connect southern China with mainland Southeast Asia (Figs. 1 and 3 and Extended Data Fig. 10).

Industry observers note that our results demonstrate that H. erectus was present in southern China between 324 and 184 ka (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 8), representing, to our knowledge, the youngest reliably dated occurrence of this species in China and the first with robust chronological constraints from southern China. The integration of multiple independent dating techniques combined with Bayesian age modelling provides unprecedented temporal resolution for late H. erectus in mainland Asia. These findings fundamentally alter our understanding of the species’ persistence and distribution in China, extending the documented record by more than 200,000 years beyond the previous youngest occurrences in Hexian and Nanjing14,15, and establishing southern China as a key region for late-surviving populations during the late Middle Pleistocene (for example, ref. 19).

Sources indicate that the temporal importance of this discovery extends beyond simply filling a chronological gap. The age uncertainty range of 324–184 ka places these H. erectus populations at some point within marine isotope stages 9 through 6, raising intriguing questions about potential contemporaneity or overlap with Homo longi (Denisovans) identified in Cobra cave (Laos)34, Baishiya cave (Tibetan Plateau)35, Harbin (northeast China)36,37,38 and the Penghu Channel off the western shore of Taiwan39. The temporal proximity of these various hominin populations across China during the late Middle Pleistocene suggests a more complex biogeographical landscape than previously recognized, with multiple hominin lineages potentially coexisting across different ecological zones and elevational gradients.

Moreover, the environmental context revealed by our multi-proxy analyses challenges prevailing assumptions about late H. erectus ecological constraints and mobility patterns. The combined evidence demonstrates unequivocally that these late H. erectus populations exploited closed-canopy tropical rainforest environments and may have conducted long-distance movement beyond the local karst terrain during childhood. The ecological implications of this rainforest use and mobility are profound. Archaeological evidence has so far suggested that H. sapiens was the only member of our genus to specialize in the regular exploitation of these environments18, as early as 150 ka in western Africa40,41. In Southeast Asia, recent isotopic observations of declines in C4 environments and expansion of rainforest in the Middle to early Late Pleistocene have been associated with the disappearance of non-H. sapiens hominin taxa42,43, seemingly unable to shift from mixed savannah–woodland habitats to these increasingly closed forests16,44. However, our data directly challenge this view by demonstrating that H. erectus was not ecologically excluded from rainforest environments (Fig. 3) and that long-distance mobility into these environments may have been a common behavioural pattern rather than exceptional behaviour by isolated individuals.

These findings contrast markedly with Early and Middle Pleistocene H. erectus occupations at Trinil3 and Sangiran in Java4 (Extended Data Fig. 9b). The youngest Javanese H. erectus at Ngandong2 persisted in relatively open woodland refugia2, leading to suggestions that expanding rainforests may have contributed to the species’ eventual extinction in Java2,16. Among early hominin-bearing sites in East and Southeast Asia (Extended Data Fig. 9b), the Naxian and Baxian cave results most closely resemble those from Lida Ajer, Sumatra (73–63 ka), an early H. sapiens site also characterized by closed-canopy rainforest45. This demonstrates that H. erectus was, at minimum, capable of persisting among rainforest fauna, even if such habitats did not represent its optimal ecological niche.

Areas in northern Vietnam, such as the Red River valley (Figs. 1 and 3), have long been recognized as a critical biogeographical corridor connecting the karst uplands of southern China with the lowlands of mainland Southeast Asia24. The limited strontium isotope evidence tentatively suggests that late H. erectus populations may have been utilizing similar corridors for seasonal movements, long-distance migrations or resource procurement. This large range (potentially around 250 km) through mostly enclosed environments challenges assumptions about the limited ranging behaviour of H. erectus and suggests behavioural sophistication in landscape use.

It has been revealed that our findings collectively demonstrate that late Middle Pleistocene H. erectus was present in southern China, surviving contemporaneously with H. longi and exhibiting considerable ecological and behavioural flexibility. Rather than being restricted to open savanna or woodland habitats, as traditionally assumed, these populations persisted in closed-canopy tropical rainforests while simultaneously engaging in potential long-distance mobility across diverse ecological and geological landscapes. This evidence challenges the characterization of H. erectus as a species unable to exploit complex tropical forest environments. Whether these adaptations were specific to the late-surviving populations in southern China alone remains to be seen, but further stable isotope work on other Middle Pleistocene sites is vital to address this question. However, the presence of morphologically and genetically confirmed H. erectus in southern China between 324 and 184 ka, combined with the environmental and suggested mobility evidence, is sufficient to necessitate a re-evaluation of the species’ adaptive capabilities, biogeographical range and ultimate fate in mainland Asia.

The caves were discovered using local knowledge and targeted reconnaissance hunting for breccia in the rear chambers. The locations of test pits within the caves were selected on the basis of these reconnaissance surveys. Excavation grids were based on the shape of cave passages and distribution of fossil-rich deposits. Jackhammers were used to break blocks of fossil breccia, and the fossils were extracted using geological hammers. Fine cleaning, identification and cataloguing were conducted in the laboratories at Shandong University and the Institute of Vertebrate Palaeontology and Palaeoanthropology (IVPP).

The fossil-bearing breccia and associated sediments from the fossil chambers of both caves were sampled in situ under subdued red-light conditions (Fig. 2a,d) and were processed using standard sample purification procedures for quartz and feldspar separation including a 40% and 10% wash in hydrofluoric acid for 45 and 10 mins, respectively46. Single aliquots of 90–125 µm feldspar and 180–212 µm quartz or feldspar grains were processed in a Riso TL-DA-20 equipped with an automated DASH set-up, a dual-laser single-grain attachment47 and a blue- and ultraviolet-sensitive Electron Tube photo-multiplier tube (PDM9107Q-AP-TTL-03), using either a blue filter pack (Schott BG-39, 2 mm, and Corning 7-59, 4 mm) for feldspars or U340 filters (2 × Hoya U340, 3.5 mm) for quartz. Data were collected using Sequence Pro v.4.65 and analysed in Analyst v.4.57, DRAC v.1.3 and on spreadsheets designed in Microsoft Excel 365 v.2607. Feldspar equivalent doses were corrected according to the results of the anomalous fading tests (using a weighted mean fading rate of 2.0 ± 0.2% per decade)48, but no residual corrections were undertaken, and the equivalent doses for both feldspar and quartz were then run through either a central age model for the single-aliquot results or a minimum age model49 to identify the single-grain population that experienced the most bleaching before burial. All luminescence analysis was conducted at the ‘Traps’ luminescence dating facility at Macquarie University in Sydney, Australia.

Recent findings suggest that measurements of 238U, 235U, 232Th and 40K were estimated using Geiger–Muller multi-counter beta counting and thick-source alpha counting of dried and powdered sediment samples in the laboratory, combined with in situ gamma spectrometry in the field. The corresponding (dry) beta and gamma dose rates were obtained using the conversion factors in ref. 50 and the beta-dose attenuation factors in ref. 51. Cosmic-ray dose rates were estimated from previously published relationships52, making allowance for the sediment overburden at the sample locality (ranging from 3.99 to 0.20 m), the altitude (ranging from 2,000 to 176 m above sea level) and geomagnetic latitude and longitude of the sampling sites.

Seven H. erectus teeth from the Naxian (n = 6) and Baxian (n = 1) caves were analysed for U-series dating across two laboratories in China and Australia. U-series measurements were undertaken using a laser-ablation multi-collector inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometer (MC-ICP-MS) at the Geoarchaeology and Archaeometry Research Group (GARG), Southern Cross University, according to protocols in ref. 53 and in a Neptune MC-ICP-MS at the School of Geography Science, Nanjing Normal University according to refs. 54,55. Laser ablation (at Southern Cross University) was performed with a Newly introduced Wave Research 213 nm laser, and thorium (230Th, 232Th) and uranium (234U, 235U, 238U) isotopes were measured on a Thermo Neptune XT MC-ICP-MS. Teeth were ablated using rasters of 5 min each and were measured with standards before and after. Uranium and thorium were separated using conventional anion-exchange chromatography at Nanjing, and the U–Th solution was then introduced into the MC-ICP-MS via a DSN-100 desolvation nebulizer system. Isotopic ratios were measured using a detector configuration that allows for the simultaneous measurement of U and Th isotopes56,57.

One H. erectus tooth and one Pongo tooth from the Baxian cave (n = 2) were selected for coupled ESR and U-series dating at GARG, Southern Cross University. Enamel fragments from each tooth were separated using a hand-held diamond saw following the protocol developed in ref. 58. Fragments were then measured at room temperature on a Freiberg MS5000 ESR X-band spectrometer at a modulation amplitude of 0.1 mT, 10 scans, 2 mW power, 100 G sweep and 100 kHz modulation frequency. Each fragment was irradiated, following exponentially increasing irradiation times. Sediment elemental concentrations, external beta and gamma dose rate contributions, and water content were obtained from in situ measurements. The external beta-dose rates have been extrapolated from the U, Th and K contents measured on a portion of sediment sub-sample (approximately 8 g). The external gamma dose rates were determined in situ using a portable gamma spectrometer at each site. The equivalent doses were estimated using Matlab-based MCdose software v.2.0.

Separate sub-samples were hand-drilled from the fresh cross-section of the in situ capping flowstones from Naxian and Baxian caves and processed at the Radiogenic Isotope Facility, University of Queensland (n = 6), and six soda straws and one sample of secondary calcite cement were processed at the School of Geography Science, Nanjing Normal University (n = 7). The powdered sub-samples were subjected to chemical treatment and isotopic measurements by mass spectrometry56. U-series dating of the speleothem samples were conducted at the University of Queensland using a Nu Plasma MC-ICP-MS, and analytical procedures followed previous publications for MC-ICP-MS57,58,59. The 230Th/234U ages were calculated using Isoplot EX 3.75 (ref. 60) and half-lives of 75,690 years for 230Th and 245,250 years for 234U (ref. 61). U-series dating of the speleothem samples was carried out at Nanjing Normal University using a Neptune MC-ICP-MS. U-series ages were calculated using the half-lives of 75,584 years for 230Th and 245,620 years for 234U (ref. 62). Non-radiogenic 230Th was corrected using an assumed bulk-Earth atomic 230Th/232Th ratio of (4.4 ± 2.2) × 10−6 (refs. 54,55).

Two Bayesian modelling programs were used to analyse selected independent age estimates (n = 43) (Supplementary Information 8) and to evaluate the uncertainties associated with the combined dating techniques applied to both sites (Supplementary Tables 7–15): OxCal (v.4.4.4, available at https://c14.arch.ox.ac.uk/oxcal.html)63 and ChronoModel (v.3.2.7, https://chronomodel.com/)64. The analyses incorporated the probability distributions of individual ages, constraints imposed by stratigraphic relationships and the reported minimum or maximum nature of some of the individual age estimates. Each individual age was included as a Gaussian distribution (with mean and s.d. defined by the age estimate and their associated uncertainties), and the resulting age ranges for each phase of deposition were presented at 2σ. OxCal allows the identification of boundary ages between each layer to constrain the fossil layer and ChronoModel was applied to assess the extent to which identical or similar data could be obtained. Both modelling results have been presented for transparency.

Three H. erectus specimens from the Naxian cave, as well as 47 faunal teeth from the Baxian cave and 38 from the Naxian cave (n = 41 in total), were taxonomically identified and prepared for stable isotope analysis, following established preparation methods65 (but see refs. 66,67). The resulting δ13C and δ18O values were measured using a ThermoFisher MAT253+ in six separate measurement blocks per sample at the Earth and Environmental Sciences’ Stable Isotope Geochemistry Laboratory at the University of Queensland. The evolved CO2 gases from the Naxian teeth were analysed for carbon and oxygen isotope compositions using a Thermo Delta V Advantage isotope ratio mass spectrometer housed at the Key Laboratory of Archaeological Sciences and Technology, Shandong University. Stable isotope measurements on the three H. erectus teeth were carried out at the Service de spectrométrie de masse isotopique du Muséum national d’Histoire naturelle, Paris, and analysed using a Thermo Delta V Advantage isotope ratio mass spectrometer. To assess isotopic differences among sites, we applied non-parametric and multivariate tests. For univariate comparisons, Kruskal–Wallis tests revealed highly significant differences in both δ13Ccarbon source (χ² = 181.5, d.f. = 6, P < 0.001) and δ18O (χ² = 114.4, d.f. = 6, P < 0.001) among sites. All statistical analyses were conducted using the open-source program R software (v.4.5.1)68.

Three in situ samples were collected in bulk (CBAX2, CBAX3, CBAX4) from the breccia at Baxian and the clumped isotope analysis was undertaken in the Macquarie GeoAnalytical Stable Isotope Facility using a ThermoFisher dual-inlet MAT253+ mass spectrometer. The results were processed using the Easotope software package69. The final Δ47 value for each sample was then averaged and reported with 95% confidence intervals, before temperatures were calculated using the calibration in ref. 70 for 90 °C reactions. Using these temperatures, the oxygen isotopic composition of the precipitating fluid (δ18Ofluid) was calculated using the equation in ref. 71.

One H. erectus tooth from Baxian was sectioned with a high-precision diamond saw and polished to a smoothness of greater than 5 μm. Laser ablation combined with ICP-MS was used for trace elemental mapping analyses using an ESI NWR193 coupled to an Agilent 7900 ICP-MS at GARG, Southern Cross University, according to the procedures in refs. 19,72. A laser spot size of 40 μm, a scan speed of 80 μm s−¹, a laser intensity of 60% (approximately 1 J mm−2) and a total integration time of 0.50 s were used to produce data points that corresponded to a pixel size of approximately 40 × 40 μm. NIST610 and NIST612 (certified standard reference materials) were used to assess signal drift. Strontium isotope analysis (87Sr/86Sr) was conducted on four H. erectus teeth: one from Baxian cave and three from Naxian cave, also using laser-ablation MC-ICP-MS at the GARG facility. Enamel fragments were carefully extracted from regions showing low uranium concentrations and distinct elemental signatures from the surrounding dentine according to the mapping results. To contextualize the 87Sr/86Sr values obtained and assess potential mobility patterns, a regional strontium isoscape was constructed for southern China and northern Southeast Asia. The isoscape modelling was based on random forest ensemble machine learning analyses adapted from the original script developed in ref. 33 and followed the method fully described in ref. 21.

All isoscapes generated using random forest machine learning were based on the global bioavailable strontium database in ref. 33 and all R scripts necessary for generating isoscapes are available at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21131183)74.

According to recent reports, K.E.W., Y.Z., R.J.-B., W.L., W.W., C.J., Y.W., W.Y., Y.P. and L.Y. explored and excavated the sites and collected faunal and dating samples, K.E.W. conducted the luminescence dating, R.J.-B., W.Y. and Q.S. conducted the U-series and coupled U-series–ESR dating of the teeth, and J.-x.Z. and Q.S. conducted the U-series measurements on the speleothem. R.J.-B. conducted the trace element analysis and V.B. conducted the isoscape work. M.Q., S.M., L.H. and A.-M.B. conducted stable isotope analysis on the fossil teeth, and N.B. and P.R. conducted isotope data analysis. M.Q. and S.M. conducted the clumped isotope analysis of the breccia, Y.Z., Y.P. and A.-M.B. analysed the fauna and K.E.W. designed the dating approach and conducted the Bayesian modelling. R.K., C.Z., W.L., R.D.Á., F.W., Z.W. and Q.F. worked on the hominin teeth. Finally, K.E.W., R.J.-B., W.L. and Y.Z. wrote the paper, with contributions from all co-authors.

Recent findings suggest that a-d Naxian cave, a and b the cave – location marked with a red star - is situated on the outer cone of a karst inselberg located close to a highway. c a montage of images to demonstrate the speleology of the cave with the small entrance and flowstone step that leads into the stalagmite chamber dense with speleothem, a larger chamber with narrow and high ceilings and terminating with a small fossil chamber with breccia, d the fossil bearing breccia at the highest point of the cave capped with flowstone and underlain by a younger underlying mixed material below. e-h Baxian Cave e and f the cave is also situated on the outer edge of a karst cone with the limestone corridor than connects both caves, cave location is marked with a red star, g a montage of images to demonstrate the speleology and sedimentology of the cave from the wide and high entrance to the narrower and smaller passage that lead to the confined fossil chamber, h the fossil bearing breccia at the highest point of the cave capped with flowstone and underlain with the younger underlying mixed material. There is a remarkable similarity between the stratigraphy and sedimentology of these deposits and associated fossils (d, h).

a Naxian profile, b Baxian profile illustrating the changing speleology and cave deposits from the upper fossil chambers down to the entrances. Baxian is longer than Naxian but slopes at a lesser angle than the steeper Naxian. Images illustrate the main features found in both caves including a wider chamber and smaller fossil chambers. The images of the fossil chambers are taken from a 3D models of the caves (Supplementary Information 2 for links).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As I left the London Stadium to a chorus of boos, I found myself desperately searching for positives from a frustrating 1-1 draw against the league’s bottom club.
  • The first was the performance of Alvarez.
  • Sources indicate that the second positive was that the statistics backed up what I’d watched unfold on the pitch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As I left the London Stadium to a chorus of boos, I found myself desperately searching for positives from a frustrating 1-1 draw against the league’s bottom club.

The first was the performance of Alvarez. Largely cast into the shadows through the stubbornness of our former manager, he grabbed the game by the scruff of the neck. He took control, lifted the crowd, and, above all, displayed the leadership qualities this team has lacked for much of the season.

Sources indicate that the second positive was that the statistics backed up what I’d watched unfold on the pitch. West Ham dominated possession with 79%, registered 30 shots, and recorded an xG of 3.13. The problem? Only four of those efforts were shots on target.

It has been revealed that we gifted Preston their opening goal. It came from a calamitous mix-up, with Piroe’s flicked header looping backwards onto the crossbar before dropping kindly for Liam Lindsay to tap home from close range. It could be argued that Herrick should have been more commanding from the corner, but he made amends later with an excellent double save.

There were concerns that we wouldn’t pull one back, we did on the 60th minute, Mavropanos heading home his sixth goal in 15 league appearances this season.

“Ifs” and “buts” don’t win football matches, and as Parker said afterwards: “The overall performance suggests we should win. The fine margins of football are, and the reality is, if Tomas Soucek scores that last-minute goal, it’s probably a different interview.”.

Industry observers note that for me, I’m not going to be negative. We needed a win and we didn’t get the three points, but what I want to see now is the team build on the domination, the chance creation and the shot volume by going to Fratton Park on Tuesday and getting the job done. If we concede first there and deliver an abject performance, then and only then will there be more serious questions to ask.

#118267. What it's really like to kill a fellow athlete - and the terrible grief 'you carry for the rest of your life': The cursed band of haunted sportsmen reveal the nightmares that never leave them

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3884 w)

What it's really like to kill a fellow athlete - and the terrible grief 'you carry for the rest of your life': The cursed band of haunted sportsmen reveal the nightmares that never leave them

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3884 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 21:00 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 22:15 EST, 19 November 2026.
  • Towards the end of the Australian summer of 2014-15, as the country prepared to host the Cricket World Cup, I took a flight from Sydney to Hobart, Tasmania, to watch a Sheffield Shield game between Tasmania and Fresh South Wales at the Bellerive Oval, a beautiful ground perched on the banks of the Derwent River.
  • Australian sport was still in shock.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By OLIVER HOLT, CHIEF SPORTS WRITER.

Published: 21:00 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 22:15 EST, 19 November 2026.

Towards the end of the Australian summer of 2014-15, as the country prepared to host the Cricket World Cup, I took a flight from Sydney to Hobart, Tasmania, to watch a Sheffield Shield game between Tasmania and Fresh South Wales at the Bellerive Oval, a beautiful ground perched on the banks of the Derwent River.

Australian sport was still in shock. A few months earlier, Australia's Test opener, Phillip Hughes, had died after he was struck on the side of his neck by a short ball from a young bowler called Sean Abbott in a game between New South Wales and South Australia at the Sydney Cricket Ground.

Hughes was treated at the ground for 40 minutes and then taken by ambulance to St Vincent's Hospital in nearby Darlinghurst in a critical condition. 'Feeling for Phil Hughes after being hit,' former Australia Test cricketer Dean Jones wrote on Twitter. 'He is not in a good way! Stay strong Sean Abbott. Not your fault, young man.'.

According to recent reports, the impact of the ball had compressed a vein in Hughes' neck and when it split, it caused a catastrophic bleed on the brain. Hughes had emergency surgery and was placed in an induced coma. He never regained consciousness and passed away two days later.

Sources indicate that hughes was a popular, talented, gutsy cricketer with three Test centuries already under his belt. A small guy with the heart of a lion. He was 25 years old. Cricket mourned a terrible tragedy – some called it the sport's saddest day and the agony of Hughes' family was hard to bear. But there was something else. There was an awareness that two tragedies were playing out in front of us.

Hughes was lost but the man who had bowled the delivery that felled him had been left behind, desolate and distraught. Many thought Sean Abbott, who was 22, would never play cricket again. That he would not be able to find the strength. But that was why I had flown to Tasmania. Because Abbott had found the strength.

Phil Hughes was the golden boy of Australian cricket in 2014, with three Test centuries already to his name, when he was hit by a ball bowled by Sean Abbott and died.

Abbott visiting the Sydney hospital where Hughes was in a coma that he would never wake from, having suffered a catastrophic bleed on the brain.

That February afternoon at the Bellerive Oval, I sat among a smattering of spectators who watched Abbott walk to the top of his mark. His team-mates shouted encouragement to him. They were willing him on with everything they had and Abbott bowled his heart out.

'Beautifully bowled, Abbo,' one of the NSW fielders shouted after one ball to former Test opener Ed Cowan. 'That's a beauty, Seanie,' another yelled after the fifth ball of his first over, when Cowan jerked his head out of the way of a short delivery so fast he fell over. Only one wicket fell that afternoon. Abbott took it.

It was one of the bravest sporting performances I have ever witnessed. Because even though cricket had voiced its support for Abbott, the sport could not protect him from his thoughts and from the knowledge he had become one of a cursed band of sportsmen who have unwittingly caused the death of an opponent during a contest.

In a recent development, sometimes, tragedy in sport is not just the tragedy of the player who dies; it is the tragedy of the opponent who must live the nightmare of what he has done over and over again in his mind. To those that it has befallen, they say it is a grief that never leaves them.

That grief, that sense of a double tragedy, was brought sharply back into focus earlier this month when Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel died in hospital the day after a sickening collision with FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono. The accident happened in the final minutes of a game in Spain's Segunda Division, when Owono hurtled out of his goal and collided with De Miguel in the centre circle. He was shown a red card for the foul.

According to recent reports, there was an outpouring of grief for De Miguel. I was among those who observed a minute's silence for him before the Barcelona-Aston Villa Champions League tie at the Nou Camp the next evening. Tributes continue to be paid to him. Owono, meanwhile, has become a pariah. It is said that the 25-year-old rarely leaves his house.

Owono does not appear to have had the same sympathy extended to him that Abbott benefited from. His challenge on De Miguel, a striker who had had a peripatetic career in Spain's lower leagues, was reckless and cavalier. For him, the struggle with guilt and responsibility and public judgment is only just beginning.

FC Andorra will play their first home game since the tragedy against Leganes on Friday night but when they run out at the Encamp Stadium, a neat little ground beside a babbling river, the Valira d'Orient, and in the shadow of the mountains that make Andorra such a popular ski resort, Owono will not be there.

Earlier this month Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel died in hospital the day after a sickening collision with FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono.

According to recent reports, owono has become a pariah. It is mentioned that the 25-year-old rarely leaves his house.

The goalkeeper, who has 47 caps for Equatorial Guinea, was given the maximum sentence of a 12-match ban by the Spanish Football Federation.

Tenerife manager Alvaro Cervera suggested Owono's ban 'might feel light' to all those mourning the striker, who was 30 years old, while FC Andorra owner Gerard Pique, the former Barcelona and Spain centre back, said the maximum sanction 'puts him (Owono) in a situation he does not deserve, because he is not to blame for all of this having happened'.

No one knows whether Owono will feel able to return to football when his ban ends. Footage circulated of him in an on-field argument moments before the clash with De Miguel, and it was used to suggest that he was in an unstable state of mind.

Some have pressed for him to be charged with manslaughter. His Instagram account was deactivated after it was deluged with abuse, including messages which branded him 'a murderer'. It has been reported that his brother, who is also a footballer, has been the victim of abuse because of his association with Owono.

Recent findings suggest that owono has only communicated through a statement released by his club. 'These are the most difficult days of my life,' he wrote. 'I struggle to find the words, and I find it very hard to ​process what has happened. I feel enormous pain at the loss of Jesus. I think of him, his family, and all the people who loved him. I know there will be many questions to address, and I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect.'.

It has been revealed that I spoke to the great British fighter Barry McGuigan about Owono this week. McGuigan has suffered his share of tragedies. His brother, Dermot, took his own life. He lost his daughter, Danika, to cancer when she was just 33, in 2019. And in 1982, three years before he won the world featherweight title at Loftus Road, he nearly quit boxing altogether.

It has been revealed that in the 12th fight of his professional career, McGuigan fought a Nigerian boxer called Young Ali at the World Sporting Club in Mayfair. He still remembers the clink of cutlery coming from the diners who were sitting ringside that night. That sound still takes him back.

McGuigan still remembers the sequence of punches that put Young Ali down in the sixth round of the fight. He saw his opponent's eyes roll back in his head and a feeling of dread washed over him. Young Ali, just 21, fell into a coma from which he never emerged and died five months later.

I spoke to the great British fighter Barry McGuigan (right) about Owono this week. McGuigan has suffered his share of tragedies.

'There was the horror of that and we sat and we waited and we prayed that he would be better and he never got better,' McGuigan told me. 'I didn't know whether I wanted to continue boxing. I thought: "If I can do this to somebody…"'.

Sources indicate that he shuddered when he talked about Owono. 'Other tragedies happen and other terrible things happen,' he said. 'Life is a struggle. Something like that, you never leave it behind you.

Industry observers note that 'It is something invisible and it depends how emotionally vulnerable he is. He may never be the same again but I hope he is able to overcome it.'.

According to recent reports, there are others out there in sport, still trying to overcome it. Think of Matt Petgrave, the Sheffield Steelers ice-hockey player who was arrested on suspicion of manslaughter after his skate fatally cut the neck of Nottingham Panthers' Adam Johnson in an Elite Ice Hockey League match at Sheffield Arena in October 2023.

Recent findings suggest that think of Jochen Mass, the Formula One driver, who spent years blaming himself for the death of Gilles Villeneuve during qualifying for the Belgian Grand Prix at Zolder in 1982, because he slowed and moved to the right in front of Villeneuve. The Ferrari ran into the back of Mass and flipped in grotesque cartwheels across the track.

Think of Matthias Behr, the German fencer who killed his opponent, Vladimir Smirnov, at the 1982 World Fencing Championships in Rome when Behr's foil blade broke during a match, penetrated the Ukrainian fencer's mask and pierced his eye.

Think of Gary Cully, the Irish fighter, who learned this week that his last opponent, Lee Reeves, had died after spending three months in a coma following their bout in Dublin in August.

'What a character and a gent,' Cully wrote in tribute to Reeves. 'It's never been nothing but love between us champ, can't really believe I'm writing this but RIP brother.'.

Nottingham Panthers' Adam Johnson died in October 2023 when opponent Matt Petgrave's skate cut his neck during a match.

Gary Cully (left), the Irish fighter, learned this week that his last opponent, Lee Reeves (right), had died after spending three months in a coma following their bout in Dublin in August.

Dr Victor Thompson, a prominent UK clinical sports psychologist, has studied the effect on competitors of being involved in the death of a rival.

Sources indicate that 'The biggest thing a player will have had to absorb normally is bad performance,' Dr Thompson states. 'Now he has to absorb the fact that he was involved in somebody dying. He will be trying to work out was it his fault? Is he to blame? And all of that, because the emotions are so high, gets associated with playing the sport in question.

'So when Sean Abbott thought about going out there again, when he thought about putting his pads on, or putting his kit on and being around team-mates or the smell of the cricket bat – it'll all be associated to that very traumatic day.'.

Recent findings suggest that university of North Carolina academic John M Silva III argued that aggression in sport is defined in two categories: hostile aggression and instrumental aggression. Hostile is when the main aim is to cause harm or injury to your opponent. Instrumental is aggression for a purpose, perhaps ball recovery or to sow doubt in an opponent’s mind.

In a recent development, the interpretation of a player's actions at a time of high stress, frustration or adversarial combat is often central to the reaction to a sporting tragedy. Whether forgiveness is extended to or opprobrium visited on the competitor who has caused the death of another.

Sources indicate that that interpretation was used against Petgrave, who was notorious for having a bad disciplinary record on the ice. Some likened the action which fatally injured Johnson to a kung-fu kick and drew a link between it and some of his past behaviour. He was mercilessly trolled on social media. Team-mates, and many ice hockey fans, leapt to his defence and said any suggestion his action was deliberate was fanciful. They said his unusual action in lifting his left skate high was a direct result of being knocked off balance by a collision.

Petgrave could not return to ice hockey immediately even if he had wanted to. It was a full 18 months before the Crown Prosecution Service and South Yorkshire Police decided there was no realistic prospect of conviction for manslaughter and that no criminal charges should be brought against the 34-year-old Canadian.

In a recent development, in the intervening period, Petgrave's family set up a crowdfunding page, pointing out that he was unable to work or to return home until the CPS had decided whether to press charges. The page raised nearly £20,000 from well-wishers.

The interpretation of a player's actions at a time of high stress, frustration or adversarial combat is often central to the reaction to a sporting tragedy - as it was for Petgrave.

Petgrave did receive widespread support from inside his sport, with a standing ovation at his Sheffield side's next home match, while he was beginning 18 months under investigation.

'This has been the most painful and overwhelming period of our lives,' a message from Petgrave's family said at the bottom of the page. 'Watching someone I love go through this has been incredibly difficult.

Sources indicate that 'Despite everything, we are doing our best to stay strong, and the support and kindness from so many people have been a source of strength. We continue to recognise the heartbreaking nature of this situation, and our thoughts remain with everyone affected. We hold on to hope that this will soon come to an end.'.

Petgrave now plies his trade in the minor league ECHL for the Indy Fuel, a team based in Fishers, Indiana. He is an ever-present this season, playing opponents like the Wheeling Nailers, the Greenville Swamp Rabbits, the Kalamazoo Wings and the Bloomington Bison.

'We understand the responsibility that comes with the great support we receive from this community,' Sean Hallett, CEO of Hallett Sports, which owns the Fuel, stated when they hired Petgrave. 'We are confident he will be a positive addition to our team and our city.'.

I wrote to the Fuel, asking if there was any chance of speaking to Petgrave. They did not respond. The reticence is understandable and, in many ways, laudable. Players involved in this kind of tragedy are preoccupied with respect for the victims' families and the sensitivities that come with such terrible grief. There is nothing they can say or do to make it better.

Sometimes, it is the other way round. Sometimes, it is the family of a lost loved one who find a way to ease the pain of a sportsman eaten up by shame for inadvertently causing the death of a competitor.

As Gilles Villeneuve's Ferrari cartwheeled across the track, breaking into pieces, he was flung clear of the wreckage still strapped to his seat, catapulting across the track.

Perhaps the fine career 2023 World Cup winner Sean Abbott (bottom right) has had is his tribute to Hughes.

Newcastle 2 Arsenal 2 match ratings and comments on all the Newcastle United players

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We asked Davey Hat-Trick to give us his match ratings and player comments after Newcastle 2 Arsenal 2 in the Premier League.
  • Out of the 1,000+ games I have watched in person, the 4-4 draw with Arsenal 15 years ago is the match that most deserves the ‘game of two halves’ label.
  • A blind man could have seen the gulf in class between the two sides in the first half.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We asked Davey Hat-Trick to give us his match ratings and player comments after Newcastle 2 Arsenal 2 in the Premier League.

Out of the 1,000+ games I have watched in person, the 4-4 draw with Arsenal 15 years ago is the match that most deserves the ‘game of two halves’ label. This one – against the same opponents – wasn’t far off.

A blind man could have seen the gulf in class between the two sides in the first half. Arsenal outclassed Newcastle without trying. Newcastle looked petrified, and it looked like no one wanted the ball. Having said that, Arsenal only scored a single goal, and didn’t really come that close again. Our centre halves were good.

It has been revealed that the second half could not have been more different. Newcastle tore into Arsenal from the get-go, and the Gunners looked shell-shocked. By the time Arsenal had recovered their composure, Newcastle were 2-1 up. In my opinion, we were playing as well as we had all season.

Arsenal were bound to come back into it, and they did. They scored an equaliser, but that’s not to say Newcastle were overwhelmed. We were giving as good as we got, and continued to do so.

Having conceded, most Geordies were fearing the traditional last-minute winner for our opponents, and when the officials came up with nine minutes of injury time, it seemed nailed on.

It has been revealed that but Newcastle held firm, and got a deserved point against the reigning champions, and this season’s most likely winners. It was a triumph of belief, effort, teamwork and quality, and it had a galvanising effect on the black and white faithful. St James’ Park was rocking to a degree I haven’t witnessed since our opener against Liverpool.

It’s hard to give the players a sensible mark. Everyone was poor in the first half. Everyone was excellent in the second.

Lukáš Horníček 5 Not at fault for Arsenal’s first, may have done better for their second, but he always looked nervy and unsure with the ball at his feet. His distribution was poor and he never looked confident.

According to recent reports, amar Dedić 4 Good player, bad game. Stranded for Arsenal’s first and took a pointless yellow card way before half time. Subbed off at half time, a bold move by the manager, but the correct one.

According to recent reports, malick Thiaw 8 If it wasn’t for our centre halves, Arsenal could have been 3-0 up at half time. Their challenges, blocks and clearances kept Newcastle in the game. Just. The second half saw Thiaw liberated to pick his passes, get up the pitch and score Newcastle’s second from all of four inches.

Recent findings suggest that dan Burn 8 A captain’s innings. Kept the Gunners from tearing us apart in the first half and made a nuisance of himself in attack in the second. I thought he wouldn’t get much game time this campaign. Now he’s one of the first names on the team sheet.

Sources indicate that lewis Hall 6 People – me included – were calling him the best left back in the world this week. I still think he is…but he wasn’t anything like that in that first half. Was mugged for Arsenal’s first and made a few other errors. He typified Newcastle’s second half – a much improved performance. Got up the pitch and had Arsenal on the back foot. Went off with what looked like a strain. Let’s hope it’s nothing serious.

In a recent development, sean Steur 5 The game passed him by in the first half and he didn’t appear for the second. I don’t think he was bad, just not particularly effective.

Industry observers note that lewis Miley 6 A mate of mine thinks he was our best player. I just thought it was a decent game from Lewis. Not exactly dominant, but decent on the ball, and another wiho improved in the second half. Had a run at goal which nearly came off.

It has been revealed that jacob Murphy 5 I only remember Newcastle having one attempt in the first half and it was Murphy who had it. It was on target as well, except it hit his own team-mate. Other than that, Jacob offered little else and was hooked at half time.

Joe Willock 6 He’d be on a 7 or 8 if he got his head up and passed the ball instead of taking on ridiculous long distance shots. I thought he had a decent game, to be fair, and was full of energy. It looked to me like he played deeper in the second half and it worked. I think he got a dodgy assist for Thiaw’s goal.

Harvey Barnes 8 Another who seemed like a bystander in the first half but who came to life in the second. Scored the goal that gave us belief and even went past his man a few times on the wing. Well played lad.

Sources indicate that william Osula 6.5 There will be some who say Osula ‘did nowt’ in the first half but I think that was due to his team-mates being pinned back in their own half. He was isolated, although he showed his usual willingness to run. Second half was a different game. His colleagues actually got up the pitch to support him and he looked much better. A good assist for our first goal and it became a more confident display.

Industry observers note that tino Livramento 7 I’d forgotten what an excellent footballer Tino can be. He came on for the second half and looked like the player we saw two seasons ago. Quick, intelligent and good on the ball. It’s fair to say the half-time substitutes improved the team; none more than Tino.

In a recent development, anthony Elanga 5.5 To be truthful, he didn’t do a lot with the ball that I remember, but he did inject pace and energy, qualities that were non-existent first half. We looked a different team. We were a different team.

Recent findings suggest that jacob Ramsey 6 We looked more secure when Jacob entered the fray. Suddenly our midfield looked better than Arsenal’s. Played some good balls but skied a shot that could have won us the game.

Recent findings suggest that yoane Wissa 4 On for a tiring Willock. Found it difficult to get into the game.

Sven Botman 5 Came on at a time when most fans’ hearts were in their mouths – Arsenal were looking dangerous. But Sven held his own and looked the part. Relief all round.

West Ham’s Draw Against Lowly Preston – 30 Shots Hide A Far Bigger Problem

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (399 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Claretandhugh

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that yesterday was a bizarre and surreal experience at the London Stadium as we watched West Ham’s half-hearted attempts to beat a stubborn Preston North End side.
  • Industry observers note that despite West Ham’s impressive array of shots, passes and corners, I never truly felt that the team had the magic or the cutting edge to win the game.
  • Alvarez- first game back in claret and blue for a year and a half.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that yesterday was a bizarre and surreal experience at the London Stadium as we watched West Ham’s half-hearted attempts to beat a stubborn Preston North End side. Sure, the Hammers had 30 shots and an impressive 79% slice of the possession pie. But scratch below the surface and there are still major problems with Scott Parker’s team, some of which I suspect will not be sorted out until the January transfer window.

Industry observers note that despite West Ham’s impressive array of shots, passes and corners, I never truly felt that the team had the magic or the cutting edge to win the game. And as crazy as it sounds, considering we’d hit the post twice and had 14 corners, I don’t actually think we threatened enough. The Hammers lacked sparkle and magic, for sure.

Alvarez- first game back in claret and blue for a year and a half.

Sources indicate that edson Álvarez was an excellent addition to the team, but he is a defensive midfielder, and realistically, the defence was improved. Herrick made a bit of a blooper in goal for the opener, but I felt he redeemed himself with an excellent double save. By and large, West Ham restricted Preston’s chances, and so we should have done. After all, they’re the worst team in the division.

Sources indicate that but our biggest problems came in attack. Edvin Austbø on the left wing flattered to deceive, cutting inside and shooting just off target at one point, but never really terrorising his marker, despite the fact that he had him on a yellow card. Joël Piroe did okay but fluffed his big chance when put through by Arne Engels.

According to recent reports, as for the supply line, Divine Mukasa flitted in and out of the game and did not create anywhere near enough, given his deployment in the number 10 position. Jarrod Bowen was wide. I mean, very wide for so much of the game that he was probably on first-name terms with the linesman. But realistically, he was just out of the game for large parts of it. We’ll get into more detail on that later.

Overall, it was nowhere near enough quality. Sure, we had momentum. Sure, we had possession. But this did not look like a group of Premier League-standard players against the worst team in the division.

And so it came to pass with Bruno Guimaraes… Newcastle United 2 Arsenal 2

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (908 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The reaction to the departure of Bruno Guimaraes seems to have overshadowed that of Alexander Isak.
  • Fans had assumed the Brazilian’s deep connection with the United faithful was mutual, so discovering it was a bit more one-sided than anyone believed, only heightened the sense of betrayal when he left for the Emirates.
  • Some writers on The Mag were asked for 50 words on Bruno Guimaraes ahead of this match; most accepting that he’s still a legend, but that the manner of his departure left a sour taste such that he shouldn’t have been immune to a tempestuous reception.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The reaction to the departure of Bruno Guimaraes seems to have overshadowed that of Alexander Isak.

Fans had assumed the Brazilian’s deep connection with the United faithful was mutual, so discovering it was a bit more one-sided than anyone believed, only heightened the sense of betrayal when he left for the Emirates.

Some writers on The Mag were asked for 50 words on Bruno Guimaraes ahead of this match; most accepting that he’s still a legend, but that the manner of his departure left a sour taste such that he shouldn’t have been immune to a tempestuous reception.

And so it came to pass; Guimaraes was roundly booed and jeered, with both his greed and his parentage loudly called into question, which felt a touch ironic, given how the faithful had once adored his father, a man who used to sit in the away end and soak up the adulation.

As it happens, Bruno was largely anonymous and replaced by the more energetic Lewis-Skelly when his side was trailing, although he hadn’t been far from converting a Declan Rice cross in the 28th minute, something that would have amounted to a low blow for most of the 52,661 crowd had his effort found its way into the back of the net.

That chance came just before Arsenal’s dominance saw them ahead. Kai Havertz dispossessed Lewis Hall high up the pitch and slid a sublime pass to Eberechi Eze, who whipped the ball past Lukas Hornicek.

Newcastle were struggling and it was what I’d expected, pre-match bonhomie with old friends and the lad, fueled by some decent ale, had swiftly evaporated when the team was confirmed.

Right on half-time, Madueke, who had already hit the base of the post in the sixth minute, passed up a golden opportunity to double Arsenal’s lead, as some of the boos that had been reserved for Bruno were now being directed at those in the black and white.

Thank goodness Matthias Jaissle had both seen enough and managed to hold his nerve, a decisive triple substitution that introduced Tino Livramento, Jacob Ramsey, and Anthony Elanga into the fray proving transformational.

It has been revealed that just four minutes after the restart, Joe Willock pressed Martin Odegaard into a costly mistake on the Arsenal left. Will Osula scooped up the loose ball and teed up Harvey Barnes, who fired clinically past David Raya to register United’s first home strike in over two months.

Barnes will tear you apart echoed around the stadium, Dedic unable to join in with the bow and arrow celebrations, Livramento now doing a better job at right back, whilst Ramsey had shored up the midfield as Steur’s replacement and Elanga looked a whole lot better than the lethargic Murphy.

Energised by a crowd that was itself suitably invigorated, United turned the game on its head.

In a recent development, in the 62nd minute, Lewis Hall’s corner was nodded back across goal by an unmarked Dan Burn. This sparked a frenetic goalmouth scramble that ended with Malick Thiaw poking home from close range, a goal confirmed after an agonising VAR check that looked at supposed handball and offside offences, that feeling of dread never materialising as Chris Kavanagh finally signalled the goal would stand.

At this stage, United were very much on top but just couldn’t muster that elusive third, and when David Raya left the field following a collision with Osula in the 70th minute, rather than worsen the Gunners evening, the long break before Kepa Arrizabalaga replaced his compatriot allowed them to regroup and turn the tide.

I’d remarked to the lad that this was going to be a long twenty minutes, possibly half an hour, for us to negotiate and somewhat inevitably, Arsenal hit us on the counter in the 78th minute.

It has been revealed that released down the flank by Odegaard, Noni Madueke cut inside to drill a shot that squirmed through Hornicek’s grasp to level the scores. Could he have saved it? Maybe, all that good work at Craven Cottage a fortnight ago undone in an instant.

At this point, had anyone feared an Arsenal winner was coming, that might have been justified, they are a very good team and their substitutions demonstrated a squad that has strength in depth.

But the final stages, including nine minutes of added time, saw both sides pushing for a winner and it’s Newcastle that will feel more aggrieved, first Kepa denied Lewis Miley before Havertz nearly scored an own goal, the crossbar coming to his rescue as the spoils were shared.

In a recent development, I wrote an article for The Mag recently highlighting that United had picked up five more points from their opening ten fixtures when making a comparison with the same fixtures from the previous campaign. You can make that six following yesterday’s gutsy performance, and you never know, Matty Jaissle might just be getting the hang of things in the St James’ hotseat.

  • West Ham hit the wood work four times and on another day could easily have romped home.
  • Nuno was ‘the tinker man’ and you’d hope Scott Parker will persevere, despite criticism and articles today demanding the immediate axing of key players.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taken in isolation yesterday’s team performance at London Stadium doesn’t look quite so poor: A draw against the bottom side who had just beaten promotion prospects Southampton symbolises everything good about this Championship: Predictable it is not.

West Ham hit the wood work four times and on another day could easily have romped home. Trouble is, after the losses and draws of recent weeks a solitary point does nothing to halt the downward slide. It does seem a little early to start demanding change to Parker’s starting eleven – who as a unit were paying together for the first time yesterday.

Nuno was ‘the tinker man’ and you’d hope Scott Parker will persevere, despite criticism and articles today demanding the immediate axing of key players.

Piroe scored on his debut – surely it is a little early to consider discarding the striker who needs a run in Parker’s side.

Footballfancast.com is typical in calling for Joel Piroe to be dropped after his poor game:.

“The left-footed attacker delivered a dismal display in the centre-forward position and must be dropped by Parker ahead of the trip to Portsmouth in midweek”.

Recent findings suggest that the real problem with that knee-jerk reaction is that there is, simply put, nobody else to fill that role: Castellanos was invisible yesterday and fluffed his one chance, a header at the far post that didn’t get within a yard of the target. Pablo is, to all intents and purposes, finished now that his benefactor Nuno has left and until January, the cupboard is bare unless Parker gambles all on one of the youngsters.

Piroe needs the same kind of run which Castellanos had in the team before discarding him: He’s already outscored the Argentine forward by 4 goals to 1 this season. Give him a break.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bruno Fernandes missed a penalty for the second successive pre-season friendly as Manchester United were beaten 4-2 by former head coach Ruben Amorim’s AC Milan.
  • Fernandes, who rolled a spot-kick wide in a shoot-out against Leeds in midweek, was gifted the chance to open his pre-season account in Wroclaw, Poland.
  • His effort was on target this time, but Milan keeper Lorenzo Torriani dived to his right to beat the shot away.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bruno Fernandes missed a penalty for the second successive pre-season friendly as Manchester United were beaten 4-2 by former head coach Ruben Amorim’s AC Milan.

Fernandes, who rolled a spot-kick wide in a shoot-out against Leeds in midweek, was gifted the chance to open his pre-season account in Wroclaw, Poland.

His effort was on target this time, but Milan keeper Lorenzo Torriani dived to his right to beat the shot away.

Fernandes did at least get an assist, taking the second-minute corner which was powerfully headed home by Harry Maguire to give United the lead.

Amorim’s Milan equalised after a defensive mix-up allowed Gonçalo Ramos to break into the area and square for Samuel Chukwueze to roll home.

United were awarded their penalty just before half-time after Koni De Winter tugged back Youri Tielemans, but Torriani guessed correctly to leave Fernandes frustrated.

United retook the lead after Patrick Dorgu pounced on a loose backpass from Filippo Terracciano, but Milan equalised again when Chukwueze’s wayward shot was poked in by Alphadjo Cissè at the far post.

Marcus Rashford, who was frozen out by Amorim and loaned out to Aston Villa and then Barcelona, came on as a substitute on the hour for his first United appearance since returning from Spain.

But Milan went ahead in the 68th minute when Chukwueze’s cross was headed home by Ramos, and three minutes later former Chelsea midfielder Ruben Loftus-Cheek raced through to hit the fourth and cap a performance that underlines United’s need for reinforcements before their season starts in earnest next Saturday, away at Hull City.

Manchester United (4-2-3-1) Lammens; Mazraoui (Dalot 61), Maguire, Heaven (Martinez 61), Shaw; Tielemans, Santos (Mainoo 61); Diallo (Lacey 61), Fernandes, Dorgu (Rashford 61); Cunha (Mbeumo 61). Subs Zirkzee, Yoro, J Fletcher, T Fletcher, Amass, Collyer, Mee (g), Heath (g), Gabriel. Booked Dorgu.

According to recent reports, AC Milan (3-4-2-1) Torriani; Terracciano (Gila 60), Winter (Vladimirov 84), Pavlovic (Diawara 84); Chukwueze, Musah (Ricci 76), Jashari (Modric 60), Estupinan (Bartesaghi 61); Loftus-Cheek (Comotto 84), Cisse (Saelemaekers 60); Ramos (Camarda 75). Subs Pittarella (g), Bouyer (g). Booked Estupinan.

Goals Chukwueze (37), Cisse (57), Ramos (68), Loftus-Cheek (71).

That six-time Champions League winner Luka Modric raised the trophy with the one hand said everything you need to know about this moment...

Aug 22: Hull City vs Manchester United.

Aug 30: Manchester United vs Ipswich Town.

Sep 6: Everton vs Manchester United.

Sep 13: Manchester United vs Manchester City.

Sep 20: Fulham vs Manchester United.

United’s pre-season ends in defeat. A wretched second half proves their undoing as Amorim’s Milan score four. Worth reminding that United led this match, twice.

Milan are playing keep-ball in these latter stages and although Mainoo regains possession, his attempt to play forward is cut out and Modric’s outside-of-the-foot pass finds Comotto, who heads straight at Lammens.

Four minutes of added time to be played...

United now raining crosses down on Milan’s box but Torriani equal to it every time.

For the second time this afternoon, Shaw directs a lovely ball into Fernandes’ path in behind Milan’s back line, but the Portugal international can’t bring it under his spell.

Industry observers note that martinez has added a little bit of urgency to United’s build-up. Mbeumo tries to feed Shaw down the line but the ball is cut out.

In a recent development, more substitutions... Diawara, Vladimirov and Comotto enter the field of play in place of Pavlovic, De Winter and Loftus-Cheek.

Sources indicate that big chance for Rashford! Martinez lofts a fantastic ball over the top but Rashford is not quite able to bring it under his spell, with Torriani and De Winter combing to clear their lines.

Milan are now sitting off, settling into a back five as they look to preserve their advantage. Fernandes, Tielemans and Dalot combine well but such has been United’s fortunes this afternoon, the ball ricochets off the referee and play is halted.

Good work from Rashford in the corner to regain possession, but his ball into the box is not picked up by a team-mate.

More changes... Ramos and Musah make way for Camarda and Ricci.

Manchester United 2 AC Milan 4 (Loftus-Cheek) No sooner had the players returned after the second-half hydration break then Milan exploit United’s exposed left side (again). Ramos sends Loftus-Cheek through and the midfielder composes himself before bending the ball around Lammens.

Manchester United 2 AC Milan 3 (Ramos) That’s too easy. United fail to learn their lesson, Shaw not getting tight enough to Chukwueze and the winger’s cross is met by newly introduced signing Ramos, who powers a header back across goal and past Lammens.

Loftus-Cheek and Ramos are doing a good job of cutting off the pass into United’s midfield in their build-up phase.

Wholesale changes on the hour mark...

Rashford (who makes his first United appearance in almost two years), Lacey, Dalot, Mbeumo, Mainoo and Martinez replace Dorgu, Amad, Mazraoui, Cunha, Santos and Heaven.

For Milan, Saelemaekers, Bartesaghi, Gila and Modric are on for Cisse, Estupinan, Terracciano and Jashari.

Manchester United 2 AC Milan 2 (Cisse) United have set a higher defensive line so far this half, with their front line pressing with more intensity to avoid the ball over the top. However Chukwueze is able to find space around the sides, coming in off the right and curling an effort goalwards which Cisse turns in at the far post. There are calls for offside, but with no VAR here, the goal stands.

It has been revealed that milan win a free-kick some 25 yards out after Fernandes clips Estupinan. Teenager Cisse steps up and fires straight into the United wall. Was always going to be difficult to trouble Lammens from there.

Sources indicate that manchester United 2 AC Milan 1 (Dorgu) United wisely decide to keep hold of the ball for a while, the midfield three rotating to disrupt Milan’s out-of-possession shape and open up passing lanes. A Milan throw-in from the right-back berth is precedes an awful backpass by Terracciano which is pounced on by Dorgu who curls the ball beyond Torriani.

United have looked bright in the opening moments of this half. They win a free-kick midway into Milan’s half. The ball is delivered to the back post and, after some 18-yard-box pinball, a relieved Torriano pounces on it.

Both teams remain unchanged as the second 45 minutes begin.

Sources indicate that all square at the break. Tough to know what to make of that half – United looked solid enough and could have taken a lead into the interval had Fernandes converted his penalty, but they failed to create a wealth of clear-cut chances. It will be interesting to see how Carrick approaches this second half.

Milan have enjoyed just a tick over two-thirds of possession, which United have contributed to in part through some lackadaisical passing.

According to recent reports, fernandes misses a spot-kick for the second time in two friendlies! Here, Torriani guesses correctly, diving to his right to palm Fernandes’ strike away.

De Winter brings down Tielemans inside the box after Terracciano loses the ball attempting to play out from the back.

Sources indicate that manchester United 1 AC Milan 1 (Chukwueze) It’s all a bit messy. Jashari causes Maguire and Santos to crash into each other (Kaka at Old Trafford, anyone?) off a throw-in, Ramos taking over with the United pair out of commission. He finds Chukwueze who finishes the move off at the far post.

The match becomes stretched momentarily as Pavlovic, the centre-back, marauds forward, setting the ball to Estupinan who delivers another dangerous cross from the left, which Lammens does well to claim.

Industry observers note that santos clips Loftus-Cheek near the byline and the referee awards Milan a free-kick. Chukwueze cuts the ball back to an unmarked Jashari on the edge of the box, but his side-footed effort flies wide.

Milan supporters unfurl a banner paying tribute to the late, great Franco Baresi, who passed away on July 31 aged 66.

Hermosa bandera a Franco Baresi.QUE EN PAZ DESCANSE, LEYENDA DEL FÚTBOL 🙏🏻 pic.twitter.com/fvE48nKVSs.

United have picked their moments to press. Santos, who has enjoyed a wonderful pre-season, is a little too overzealous in his attempts to regain possession and gives away a foul. But the intent is correct.

Shaw floats a delightful ball over the top for Fernandes to gallop on to. The Portuguese steals in ahead of De Winter but cannot find the target with his weaker left foot.

Cisse escapes the clutches of Mazraoui down the left and fires a shot (more likely a mis-hit cross) straight into the gloves of Lammens.

United finally get their foot on the ball, but Heaven attempts an ambitious cross-field pass and possession goes back to the Italians.

In a recent development, A Mexican wave has already begun. We’re only 21 minutes in...

Industry observers note that carrick’s side continue to sit off, allowing Milan to keep hold of the ball. Cisse works in from the left, playing a neat one-two with Ramos before his curled strike sails well over.

A period of extended possession for Milan, United dropping into a compact 4-4-2 mid-block. Estupinan rains in a dangerous cross from the left and the ball falls to Loftus-Cheek, whose effort is expertly saved by the right boot of Lammens.

In a recent development, estupinan goes into the book after pulling Amad’s shirt as he looked to dart in behind after Tielemans had played a dangerous through-ball. Might possibly have been the last man?

Tielemans cedes possession to the busy Jashari just outside his own box, the Swiss midfielder moving the ball on to Loftus-Cheek who fires a shot straight at Lammens.

It has been revealed that amad picks Pavlovic’s pocket and the Milan centre-half is forced to concede a corner. United unable to score from this one.

Recent findings suggest that milan are indeed in Amorim’s preferred 3-4-2-1 formation. They circulate the ball in front of United’s first line of pressure in an attempt to calm things down.

Manchester United 1 AC Milan 0 (Maguire) Fernandes delivers an inswinger from the left and Maguire is there to meet it at the back post, striding past Musa to plant a header past Torriani.

United make a fast start, Dorgu flashing a cross-cum-shot across the face of goal. Torriani gets a fingertip to it and thte ball goes behind for a corner.

According to recent reports, szymon Marciniak, the experienced Polish referee, gets us under way. Milan send the ball back to goalkeeper Torriani.

In a recent development, the players emerge from the tunnel, United debuting their lovely new cream third kit and Milan in their traditional red-and-black home colours. Smoke machines and pyrotechnics add to the atmosphere in Wroclaw...

In a recent development, we are almost ready to go. Let us know your match predictions and thoughts on United’s prospects this season in the comments section beneath this blog.

Manchester United defeated Leeds United on penalties to hoist the mighty Boyle Sports Cup at Croke Park. The match, a 1-1 draw, was brought to an abrupt end after five young pitch invaders ran to the middle of the field to take selfies with Bruno Fernandes. In the shoot-out it was James Justin who missed the “decisive” spot-kick, paving the way for Noussair Mazraoui to win it for United.

According to recent reports, marcus Rashford is on the bench this afternoon and could make his first United appearance since his cameo in a Europa League win over Viktoria Plzen in December 2024. He was frozen out under Amorim and has since been loaned to Aston Villa and Barcelona, but his Old Trafford future under Carrick remains unclear.

Michael Carrick believes Manchester United can push for the Premier League title, but has underlined the urgent need for signings.

The United head coach has taken heart from his squad’s promising preparations for the fresh campaign and, speaking at their Co Kildare summer base, he explained why he was confident they could build on last season’s third-place finish.

It has been revealed that carrick has been thrilled to hear United’s players discussing what they might achieve and has dared supporters to dream that they can get closer to last year’s champions Arsenal. But he is also a realist and recognises he is not blessed with options.

So far United have added Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Karl Darlow, a reserve goalkeeper, but their £83.3m spend is significantly less than what newly promoted clubs Ipswich Town (£109.4m) and Coventry City (£92.2m) have invested in their squads.

Amorim’s side have gone intercontinental this summer, travelling from Scotland to Indonesia, via Australia, before arriving in Poland for the last of their four pre-season games.

Aug 5: AC Milan 1 Inter Milan 1.

In memory of Franco Baresi 🇮🇹♾️ pic.twitter.com/ULAJRjxDvE.

It has been revealed that at his AC Milan unveiling, Amorim was asked about the learnings from his United tenure that he would take into his upcoming role. He said: “The first thing is it’s hard to explain the mistakes because for that I would have to explain the context of the last adventure.

Sources indicate that “It’s hard to say to you every mistake. The only thing I can say is that I learned a lot and I made some mistakes.

“I didn’t have the opportunity, and I’m sorry for that, I didn’t have the opportunity to say something to the Manchester United fans at the moment and I’m really proud to be their coach for a year in that time.

It has been revealed that “But now it’s a different history. There are a lot of things that I could do better in the last experience but sometimes it’s like that, you need to learn to find the right spot to reach a different level and that’s my thinking here.

Recent findings suggest that “Everyone learns from their experience. I learned a lot, I did some mistakes I will try to change, there are some thing you will never change but I think I will be a better manager, that’s all.”.

Welcome to live coverage of Manchester United’s final pre-season match, against AC Milan in Wroclaw, Poland. Michael Carrick’s side will look to apply the finishing touches to a promising summer on the pitch, which has included victories over Rosenborg and Atlético Madrid, plus a draw against European champions Paris St-Germain. The team will fly back to Manchester with the significant ones, the ones they have always wanted – the Snapdragon Cup and the Boyle Sports Cup – in tow.

In a recent development, at the Tarczynski Stadium there will be a reunion with former manager Ruben Amorim, who was appointed AC Milan’s head coach in June, five months after being sacked by United. Following a frustrating season under Massimiliano Allegri in which Milan fell out of the Champions League spots on the final day, the Rossoneri remarked Amorim would bring a “modern dominant tactical approach”. His methods failed to cut through at Old Trafford, though, during a tumultuous 14-month reign which finally ended after the Portuguese “blew up” during a heated meeting with director of football Jason Wilcox. At Milan, Amorim has persisted with the 3-4-2-1 formation that was doomed at United.

Carrick made clear this week that United must strengthen if they are to challenge for titles. So far the club have brought in Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Karl Darlow, but they are still in the market for a left-back and another midfielder. The future of Marcus Rashford has also been a topic of conversation among United fans. The forward has not played for his boyhood club since December 2024 but has joined up with his team-mates in Poland and it remains to be seen if he features in Carrick’s forward planning.

Kobbie Mainoo, who did not play a minute at this summer’s World Cup, and Lisandro Martínez have also joined up with the team this week and could be handed their first minutes of pre-season having been named in the matchday squad. For Milan, newly introduced signing Gonçalo Ramos – bought from PSG for £63m – will make his first appearance in the famous red and black.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An increase to the St James’ Park capacity was officially revealed by Newcastle United, this news came on the Friday (21 August 2026) afternoon ahead of the Liverpool match.

The Newcastle United owners announcing the St James’ Park increased capacity as part of a number of improvements (see below).

It has been revealed that the official announcement stating: ‘We’ve expanded our safe standing provision with the introduction of new safe standing areas on Level 7. Thanks to additional work carried out by our operations team, we’ve also increased stadium capacity by approximately 500 seats, taking St. James’ Park’s capacity to 52,719 – enabling more supporters to experience live football in person.’.

Obviously not the tens of thousands increase in stadium capacity that we are all waiting to hear about BUT every little helps. Up to another 500 Newcastle United fans extra able to get into each St James’ Park match.

For the Liverpool match it was a upcoming Premier League era home record attendance for Newcastle United, a crowd of 52,630.

That St James’ Park record in the Premier League era was then broken again when 52,643 was the official attendance for the Bournemouth game on 5 September.

Then on September 19 against Hull City, the PL era record at SJP broken yet again, with 52,647 inside St James’ Park.

Now on Saturday 21 November for the 2-2 draw with Arsenal, edging up to 52,661.

That 21 August 2026 announcement also included: ‘We’ve invested £10 million into our hospitality offering, delivering one of the most extensive upgrade programmes ever undertaken at St. James’ Park. Highlights include full refurbishments of the Chairman’s Suite, and transformation of The Magpie into a stunning upcoming pitch view hospitality space, Tidings. Plus, we’ve reimagined Heroes into Icons, which is a tribute to Newcastle United legends and inspired by one of the club’s most iconic retro kits. Additional improvements have been made across the Barracks, Four Corners and Moncur Suites, alongside the transformation of 22 executive boxes.’.

Sources indicate that the St James’ Park pitch also having money spent on it: ‘This summer has also seen a significant investment in the heart of the stadium, with £3.6 million invested in a brand-newly introduced pitch structure; the first complete replacement in 21 years. The project includes the installation of a state-of-the-art SubAir system, helping to maintain playing conditions throughout the season.’.

The club also detailing: ‘Over the summer, we’ve completed a stadium-wide PA system upgrade and invested £2 million in a new LED floodlighting system, complete with a backup generator to improve resilience.

It has been revealed that work has also continued on improving mobile connectivity through the rollout of full stadium 5G infrastructure, helping supporters stay connected on matchdays. We’ve also installed four new in‑bowl replay screens, enhancing visibility of replays and key moments during games for supporters across the stadium.’.

💡 Key Takeaways
